title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as Savings
dek: The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take is still money you should take.
why: Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the public sector, is especially informative.
who: Employees with a provident fund who aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a provident fund loan, or contributing as flexible-employment workers; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chat about how the episode came about and where the three hosts stand can be fast-forwarded; start at 13:10 with Zhou Yi's account of actually using it.

points.h: Six months into automatic withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi turned on Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2,000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran out at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, which only added friction to daily life. Once she confirmed the fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai noted this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can and use everything you can’, and two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian cautioned that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine — people will always cook the books for themselves.

points.h: The provident fund is not savings; not being able to withdraw is the norm
points.body: Yubai walked through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the provident fund, but the home is self-occupied, so it qualifies neither as buying nor as renting; even if the new rules allow withdrawal under the heading of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs there is nothing to be done. If you risk it and invent a pretext for fraudulent withdrawal, you will be pursued to return the entire amount and barred from withdrawing any provident fund for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate higher than a demand deposit’ — and the key is the individual's situation.

points.h: The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal scope
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating a self-occupied home and paying property fees on a self-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the fund no longer serves only the single purpose of a mortgage. Second, renting used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal scope. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management center must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being pushed forward.

points.h: The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: The figure Lao Qian saw: this year, the share of provident fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, against more than 70% at the peak — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules aim at housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation both withdrawable, thresholds sharply lowered — supporting measures as the property market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the ageing trend: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly when the post-1960 cohort retired.

points.h: If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing
points.body: Yubai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou has several caps, and at application the smallest of the standards applies: for a first or second self-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so a 1 million yuan home can't be loaned more than 800,000; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is also disallowed. So before withdrawing the fund as living expenses, check your city's lending rules. Yubai is also cautious about the buy-side logic that ‘the rental yield is close to the provident fund rate, only the down payment is missing’: you still have to consider depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 yuan down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: The contribution base and rate for flexible-employment workers are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: 10,000 yuan at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money is not counted in individual income tax, but it's a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a provident fund loan, and most do not allow one-off back payments.

points.h: In the public sector, the provident fund is invisible welfare
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public-institution post back home, who readily showed a screenshot of the account: the monthly deposit is more than twice hers, and the balance already exceeds her savings; the friend lives at home with no need to rent, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus a职业年金 on top, with bonuses and allowances all counted into the contribution base. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, whereas individual pension contributions are capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal — the public sector simply has an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the national average annual wage for urban non-private units was 129,441 yuan, for private units 71,590 yuan, while working hours run the other way.

points.h: Full provident fund contributions are a lens on a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ has not changed at all: a company that contributes in full respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run across the board and won't play cat-and-mouse with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi did the math: on a wage base of 100, you take home just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130, and everyone along the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's pay raise on the Model T — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was simply a better utility function.

quotes.text: It arrives, but because your phone gets so many app notifications you don't look carefully — say it tells you 2,000 yuan came in, and it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is already used up and it gets auto-deducted from that card.
But the fact is people cook the books for themselves, people withdraw on impulse for all sorts of reasons, people are very good at self-deception.
You really can't treat the provident fund as a deposit, because your bank deposit you can withdraw at any time, but the provident fund you can't.
And it's the highest-quality lending channel, the rate is so low, yet only a bit over 30% of people actually took a loan — and at the peak it was over 70% — in just a few short years.
I think a company that contributes the provident fund in full shows it respects its employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean higher costs — it also means one person's spending, the household sector's spending, becomes the corporate sector's income, and the corporate sector's spending becomes the household sector's wages; the two form a virtuous cycle.
Take everything you can and use everything you can — buying a home, building, renovating, repaying a loan, renting, retirement, leaving the country — all of it can be used.
